title: Not Just Home Life: A Critical Mass of Belief-Supporting Contexts
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart challenges teachers who quietly write off students who combine a tough home life with low motivation. The assumption behind that is that one hour a day cannot compete with years of hardship, which he concedes holds a sliver of truth but not the whole story. He proposes that five student beliefs, about teacher credibility, the value of the work, the payoff of effort, efficacy, and belonging, remain malleable and can be shifted in a single class period, according to the research he cites. Children from difficult homes are harder to motivate chiefly because they lack years of belief-building at home. His school-level conclusion is that leaders should surround such students with as many belief-supporting contexts as possible, from teachers to coaches to parents, because a critical mass is what makes the beliefs stick and begins to deliver equity.
points: Writing off unmotivated students from hard homes, whether through friendship or neglect, is a failure of expectations.
Five beliefs (credibility, value, effort, efficacy, belonging) drive motivation and can be influenced within a classroom.
The main handicap of a tough home is missing years of belief-cultivation, not an unchangeable deficit.
Schools should train every adult, including coaches and support staff, to build belief-supporting contexts across the whole day.
A critical mass of consistent contexts is what makes beliefs durable and mitigates home disadvantage.
quotes: Here’s what I think: We assume that sixty minutes in class per day can’t overturn what’s been wrought by however many years in a tough, demotivating home environment.
Our rooms are not the center of our students’ universes; we are not omnipotent. The kid who spends one hour with me a day spends 23 hours elsewhere, still living her life.

I’m just saying that we can cultivate them. They are malleable. Dave Yeager is one of many researchers who has demonstrated that key beliefs can be durably influenced in as little as a single class period.

From a student motivation perspective, the biggest disadvantage of coming from a tough home is that you miss out on years’ worth of belief-cultivation opportunities. In my own home, I look for any chance I can to help my kids believe in their teachers (Credibility), value school and learning (Value), focus on their effort (Effort), think wisely about success (Efficacy), and see themselves as the kinds of people who apply themselves in school and treat others with kindness (Belonging).

But second, if you want to create a school or a system that transforms low motivation/tough home life kids into learners, then Job #1 is creating as many belief-supporting contexts in the school day as possible. You want your teachers to understand the beliefs, how they work, how they get undermined inside and out.

When kids are inundated with systems and procedures and messages and learning experiences that cultivate these beliefs, tough home circumstances won’t be erased, but they will be mitigated. Equity starts here.
